title: Canada | Bank Act Financial Consumer Protection Framework and FCAC
tagline: Apply Part XII.2 of the Bank Act in a Canadian bank: fair sales, consent, disclosure, basic banking, complaints, whistleblowing and FCAC enforcement.
sectors: Federally regulated banks and authorized foreign banks
Bank compliance, complaints and learning functions
description:
This quest teaches the market conduct rules that the **Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC)** supervises in federally regulated banks. It is built on **Part XII.2 of the Bank Act** (the Financial Consumer Protection Framework, in force since 30 June 2022), the **Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations**, the **whistleblowing provisions in sections 979.1 to 979.4**, the **Financial Consumer Agency of Canada Act** and FCAC's guidelines on appropriate products and services, complaint handling and whistleblowing.

Section **627.02** of the Bank Act requires every bank to train its officers and employees in Canada, and anyone who offers or sells its products in Canada, on the policies and procedures it uses to comply with the consumer provisions. This quest is designed as that periodic training for all staff and third-party sellers, with extra depth for sales, complaint and compliance roles. It also explains the **consumer-targeted fraud duty in section 627.134**, which has been enacted but is **not yet in force**.

You follow a fictional team at Aurora Ridge Bank in Toronto, Montréal, Winnipeg, Mississauga and Vancouver, and study real FCAC enforcement decisions.

This quest builds knowledge of the law and good practice; it does not replace your institution's own policies, procedures or advice from your compliance team.
audience: All officers and employees in Canada of banks, authorized foreign banks and federal credit unions
Branch, contact centre and digital staff who open accounts and sell deposit, card and credit products
Third parties who offer or sell bank products, such as brokers, dealers and retail partners
Complaint handlers, designated complaint employees and whistleblowing report handlers
Product, incentive, compliance and learning teams who design and evidence the training programme
outcomes: Explain Part XII.2 of the Bank Act, FCAC's role and the section 627.02 training duty for staff and third-party sellers
Apply the rules on undue pressure, coercive tied selling, appropriate products, remuneration and express consent
Apply disclosure rules and the right to a retail deposit account, including the narrow grounds for refusal
Handle complaints within the 56-day period, explain escalation to OBSI and apply the whistleblowing protections
Describe the consumer-targeted fraud duty in section 627.134 and its not-yet-in-force status accurately
Explain FCAC's enforcement tools and the evidence a bank needs to show an effective training programme

cards.title: Stage one: the binder on Nadia's desk
cards.setting: Consumer Protection Office, Aurora Ridge Bank head office, Bay Street, Toronto. 8:40 am.

lines.text: Your first morning as consumer protection training coordinator at Aurora Ridge Bank, a fictional federally regulated bank with branches from Halifax to Vancouver.
Welcome! I'm Nadia Haddad, Chief Compliance Officer. This binder is our map of Part XII.2 of the Bank Act. Your job is to make every page of it real for 4,000 people.
Étienne Gagnon, branch manager in Montréal. Honest question: my tellers already do AML and privacy modules. Why another one?
Because the Bank Act itself says so. Section 627.02 requires us to train officers, employees and anyone who sells our products on the policies we use to meet the consumer provisions.
Mei Chen, products and incentives, Vancouver. Does that include the mortgage brokers and the retail partner that sells our co-branded card?
Good question. Hold it. By the end of this stage you'll know who is in scope, who checks, and what happens when training fails.

cards.title: Canada's consumer protection framework in five scenes

scenes.heading: One Act, one Part
scenes.narration: Since 30 June 2022, Part XII.2 of the Bank Act, called Dealings with Customers and the Public, holds the main federal consumer rules for banks and authorized foreign banks.

scenes.heading: Regulations add detail
scenes.narration: The Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations fill in details the Act leaves to regulation, such as the 56-day period for dealing with complaints and the prescribed debt collection practices.

scenes.heading: FCAC supervises
scenes.narration: The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada supervises banks' compliance with these consumer provisions. OSFI looks after safety and soundness; FCAC looks after how customers are treated.

scenes.heading: Guidelines explain expectations
scenes.narration: FCAC guidelines on appropriate products, complaint handling and whistleblowing say how FCAC expects banks to meet the law. Where an older guideline conflicts with the framework, the framework prevails.

scenes.heading: Training ties it together
scenes.narration: Section 627.02 requires the bank to train its officers, employees and third-party sellers on the policies and procedures it set up to comply. Policies nobody knows about protect nobody.

cards.title: How Part XII.2 is organised
cards.caption: Five divisions. Most of what front-line staff do every day sits in Divisions 2 and 3.

items.label: Division 1: Interpretation
items.detail: Definitions such as complaint, undue pressure and retail deposit account

items.label: Division 2: Fair and equitable dealings
items.detail: Training, prohibited conduct, appropriateness, consent, basic banking, credit, complaints and the external complaints body

items.label: Division 3: Disclosure and transparency
items.detail: Clear, simple, not misleading information, information boxes, advertising, branch closure notices

items.label: Division 4: Redress
items.detail: Credit or refund of charges imposed without agreement or consent

items.label: Division 5: Regulations
items.detail: Power to make the detailed rules found in the Framework Regulations

cards.question: A teller at Aurora Ridge Bank asks which body supervises whether the bank follows the Bank Act consumer provisions. What is the best answer?
options: The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC)
The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI)
FINTRAC, Canada's financial intelligence unit
The provincial securities commission where the branch is located
cards.explanation: The FCAC Act makes supervising financial institutions' compliance with the consumer provisions one of FCAC's objects. OSFI is the prudential supervisor and FINTRAC deals with money laundering and terrorist financing.

cards.title: Section 627.02: who must be trained, on what
cards.body:
The training duty is short but wide.

- **Who:** officers and employees **in Canada**, plus **any person who offers or sells** the bank's products or services in Canada. That reaches brokers, agents and retail partners, not only staff.
- **On what:** the bank's own **policies and procedures** for complying with the **consumer provisions**, so the content must follow the bank's real processes, not a generic slide deck.
- **How often:** the Act sets no cycle. The map classifies this programme as mandatory with a periodic refresh, and FCAC guidelines expect **initial and ongoing** training for selling, complaint handling and whistleblowing.

Section 627.15 adds that a bank may only use representatives, agents, intermediaries or certain affiliates to sell its products if they follow the consumer provisions, give customers access to the bank's complaint process and give their employees access to whistleblowing procedures.

cards.title: In scope for section 627.02 training?
cards.prompt: Decide whether each person must be trained on Aurora Ridge Bank's consumer protection policies.

items.text: A part-time teller in the Halifax branch
A mortgage specialist who works from home in Calgary
Staff of a retail partner that sells the bank's co-branded credit card in Canada
A senior vice-president in Toronto who approves new fee structures
A contact centre agent in Winnipeg who opens accounts by phone
A bank employee working only at its London, England office on non-Canadian business
A customer's own accountant who reviews their bank statements

cards.title: A turn: the rebate nobody entered

lines.text: Before we design anything, read this. FCAC summary of proceeding number 2, posted in November 2024.
Priya Raman, complaints lead. I remember it. Card customers did not get the annual fee rebate they were entitled to.
FCAC said employees did not enter the rebate properly because procedures were inadequate. About 256,000 customers over roughly 22 years.
So a manual step, done wrong by people who were never shown how, turned into a penalty?
Exactly. That is why section 627.02 matters. Procedures and training are controls, not paperwork.

cards.title: Real case: TD and the missing card fee rebate (2024)
cards.body:
FCAC's **Summary of proceeding #2** (posted November 2024) reports that on 11 July 2024 **the Toronto-Dominion Bank** paid a **$6.5 million** penalty.

- TD was deemed to have violated the Cost of Borrowing (Banks) Regulations (2001 to June 2022) and then the **Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations** (June 2022 to October 2023).
- Monthly card statements were wrong because **employees did not properly enter the annual fee rebate**, owing to **inadequate procedures**.
- FCAC estimated about **255,886 customers** affected, with a financial impact of about **$71.7 million**; TD was reimbursing customers.
- FCAC said the penalty reflected negligence in failing to put in place controls and compliance monitoring for over 20 years, the harm caused and TD's history of violations.

**Lesson:** a step that depends on staff needs a clear procedure, training on it and monitoring that would catch errors.

cards.title: The partner who wants to skip training
cards.situation: Mei is launching a co-branded credit card with a national electronics retailer. The retailer's sales staff will take card applications at the checkout. The retailer's manager says: 'Our people are sales experts. We'll hand out your brochure, but we don't have time for your bank's training.' The launch date is in three weeks.

choices.text: Require the retailer's sellers to complete the bank's training on its consumer policies before they take applications, and build this into the partner agreement with completion tracking.
choices.outcome: Best choice. The retailer's staff offer and sell the bank's product in Canada, so section 627.02 reaches them, and section 627.15 requires intermediaries to follow the consumer provisions. Tracking completion gives the bank evidence.

choices.text: Let them start, but send the training link and ask them to complete it within six months.
choices.outcome: Partly right. Training will eventually happen, but months of sales by untrained sellers create exactly the consent and pressure risks the framework targets.

choices.text: Accept the manager's view: the brochure carries the disclosures, so training adds little.
choices.outcome: Poor choice. Disclosure documents do not replace training. The Act requires anyone who offers or sells the bank's products in Canada to be trained on the bank's policies.

choices.text: Ask the retailer to sign a statement that its staff know Canadian consumer law.
choices.outcome: Weak. A statement is not training on the bank's own policies and procedures, and it gives FCAC no evidence of what sellers were taught.

cards.title: FCAC and OSFI: two federal supervisors of a bank
cards.caption: Both supervise the same federally regulated bank, through different lenses.

items.label: Main focus
items.left: Market conduct and treatment of consumers

items.label: Key law
items.left: Bank Act Part XII.2 and the FCAC Act
items.right: Bank Act prudential parts and the OSFI Act

items.label: Whistleblowing
items.left: Employees may report wrongdoing to the Commissioner
