cards.title: Key terms of the framework

cards.back: The provisions of the Bank Act and other laws that FCAC supervises for the protection of consumers, including Part XII.2.
In Part XII.2, a bank or an authorized foreign bank. FCAC's guidelines note that banks include federal credit unions.
Dissatisfaction, whether justified or not, expressed to the bank about a product or service or how it was offered, sold or provided.
Pressure, through a practice, a communication or otherwise, that could reasonably be considered excessive or persistent in the circumstances.
Regulations made under the Bank Act, in force since 30 June 2022, that set the detailed rules, such as the 56-day complaint period.
FCAC's statement of how it expects banks to meet a legal requirement, for example the Guideline on Appropriate Products and Services.

cards.question: Aurora Ridge Bank uses an independent mortgage broker firm to bring in mortgage customers in Ontario. Under section 627.15, what must be true before the bank may cooperate with such an intermediary to sell its products?
options: The intermediary follows the consumer provisions as if it were the bank, and its customers can use the bank's complaint procedures
The intermediary has its own licence, so the bank's consumer rules no longer apply to those sales
Only the bank's own staff are covered, so the intermediary needs no arrangements
The intermediary must send all complaints directly to FCAC for resolution
cards.explanation: Section 627.15 lets the bank use representatives, agents, intermediaries and certain affiliates only if they comply with the consumer provisions that apply to them, customers have access to the bank's complaint procedures, and their employees can use the whistleblowing procedures. FCAC does not resolve individual complaints.

cards.title: Real case: BMO and the fee waiver start date (2025)
cards.body:
FCAC's **Summary of proceeding #4** (posted February 2026) reports that on 22 April 2025 the **Bank of Montreal** paid a **$4 million** penalty for two violations of its **Bank Act disclosure obligations** on personal deposit accounts.

- Customers in discounted banking programs for newcomers, medical and dental students, Indigenous banking clients and a home financing promotion who applied **in branch** got written confirmation with the **wrong start date** for their fee waiver, so they paid fees that should have been waived or discounted.
- FCAC said the root cause was **inconsistent employee adherence to procedures** and monitoring and controls that failed to detect it.
- BMO estimated about **101,091 customers** were financially affected and refunded about **$3.0 million**.
- The penalty reflected BMO's negligence, **despite over 500 customer complaints** about the fees.

**Lesson:** training is only effective if people follow it, and monitoring checks that they do.

cards.title: Stage one take-aways
items: Part XII.2 of the Bank Act, Dealings with Customers and the Public, has been in force since 30 June 2022, with detail in the Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations.
FCAC supervises banks' compliance with the consumer provisions; OSFI supervises prudential soundness.
Section 627.02 requires training of officers and employees in Canada and anyone who offers or sells the bank's products in Canada, on the bank's own consumer policies and procedures.
Section 627.15 extends consumer, complaint and whistleblowing protections to intermediaries and certain affiliates that sell the bank's products.
Recent FCAC penalties against TD and BMO trace back to inadequate procedures, staff not following them and weak monitoring.

cards.prompt: List the products you offer or support. For each, which bank policy or procedure tells you how to treat the customer, and when were you last trained on it?

quiz.question: Since what date has Part XII.2 of the Bank Act (the Financial Consumer Protection Framework) applied to banks?
options: 1 January 2020
30 June 2018
23 June 2027
30 June 2022
quiz.explanation: FCAC's guidelines page and the Framework Regulations confirm that the framework came into force on 30 June 2022. 23 June 2027 is the effective date of the revised complaint-handling guideline, not of the framework.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the training duty in section 627.02 of the Bank Act?
options: Train officers and employees in Canada, and anyone selling its products in Canada, on its consumer policies
Only branch staff who open deposit accounts must complete an FCAC-approved course every year, with results filed with FCAC
Each employee must personally pass an FCAC examination before dealing with customers, and repeat it every two years
Only the Chief Compliance Officer must be trained, and must then brief the board on consumer policies once a year
quiz.explanation: Section 627.02 covers officers and employees in Canada and any person who offers or sells the bank's products or services in Canada. FCAC does not approve courses or examine individual staff.

quiz.question: A product manager at Aurora Ridge Bank says: 'Section 627.02 only covers people with customer-facing jobs, so I'm exempt.' What is the best response?
options: Correct, the duty only applies to people who meet customers face to face in a branch or by phone in Canada
It covers all officers and employees in Canada, so product staff must be trained too
Correct, but only if the product manager earns sales commissions on the products the bank sells in Canada
The section covers product staff only if they hold a provincial licence to sell insurance or securities
quiz.explanation: The text refers to the institution's officers and employees in Canada, without limiting it to customer-facing roles. Product managers design fees, disclosures and sales processes that the consumer provisions govern.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between FCAC's and OSFI's roles towards a federally regulated bank?
options: FCAC supervises capital, liquidity and governance; OSFI handles customer complaints and sales practices
FCAC resolves individual customer complaints; OSFI writes the consumer provisions and approves bank training
FCAC supervises market conduct and the consumer provisions; OSFI supervises prudential safety and soundness
There is no real difference; the two agencies share every supervisory task for banks equally
quiz.explanation: FCAC's objects include supervising compliance with the consumer provisions. OSFI is the prudential regulator. FCAC itself says it does not resolve individual complaints.

quiz.question: Aurora Ridge Bank pays a car dealership to offer its auto loans to customers in Canada. The dealership's finance staff have never seen the bank's consumer policies. Which provisions are most directly engaged?
options: Only the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, since loans carry laundering risk
None, because the dealership is not a bank and its finance staff are entirely outside the Bank Act
Sections 627.02 and 627.15: sellers must be trained and must follow the consumer provisions
Only section 979.4, which bans retaliation against employees who report wrongdoing at the bank
quiz.explanation: The dealership offers and sells the bank's product in Canada, so its staff fall within section 627.02, and section 627.15 requires such intermediaries to comply with the consumer provisions. The anti-retaliation rule is a separate duty.

quiz.question: An older FCAC guideline says one thing and the Framework Requirements in the Bank Act and the Framework Regulations say another. According to FCAC, which prevails for a bank's conduct after 30 June 2022?
options: The older guideline prevails because it is more detailed
The Framework Requirements prevail over the older guideline
The bank may choose whichever is more convenient
Neither applies until FCAC issues a ruling to that bank
quiz.explanation: FCAC's guidelines page states that from 30 June 2022 the affected guidelines must be read with, and subject to, the Framework Requirements, which prevail in case of inconsistency.

quiz.question: In FCAC's 2024 summary of proceeding about TD's credit card annual fee rebate, what did FCAC identify as the cause of the error?
options: Employees did not properly enter the rebate because procedures were inadequate
A cyber attack that changed rebate amounts on statements sent to customers
Customers who failed to ask for the rebate within the time set in their agreement
A change in federal tax law that removed the rebate for most cardholders
quiz.explanation: FCAC said the statements were wrong because employees did not properly enter the annual fee rebate due to inadequate procedures, and noted the absence of effective controls and monitoring for over 20 years.

quiz.question: Which body of rules gives the detailed requirements under Part XII.2, such as the period for dealing with complaints?
options: The Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations
OSFI's Guideline E-21 on operational risk
The Canada Labour Code
The Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations
quiz.explanation: The Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations (SOR/2021-181) set detailed rules under Part XII.2, for example the 56-day period for dealing with complaints.

quiz.question: Mei proposes to train the co-branded card partner's sellers using a generic 'Canadian consumer law' video bought online. What is the main weakness?
options: Videos are not allowed as a training format under the Bank Act or FCAC's guidelines on training
Partner sellers need no training at all, so any content for them is unnecessary under the Bank Act
FCAC requires all consumer protection training to be delivered face to face in a classroom setting
The Act requires training on the bank's own policies and procedures, which it will not cover
quiz.explanation: The duty is to train people on the policies and procedures the bank has established to comply with the consumer provisions. Generic content may help, but it cannot show sellers how the bank's own processes work. The Act does not prescribe a format.

quiz.question: In the BMO fee waiver case (FCAC summary of proceeding #4), which factor did FCAC highlight when explaining the penalty?
options: BMO had refused to refund any of the customers who were charged the wrong monthly plan fees
BMO had deliberately set the wrong waiver start dates to raise fee revenue from newcomers
BMO had no complaint-handling procedures at all and had never filed them with FCAC
Its controls missed the error despite more than 500 customer complaints about the fees
quiz.explanation: FCAC pointed to BMO's negligence in failing to implement adequate controls and monitoring, despite receiving over 500 complaints about the monthly plan fees. BMO did refund affected customers.

sessions.title: Fair dealing: appropriate products, undue pressure, tied selling and consent
sessions.summary: Apply the Bank Act rules on misleading information, undue pressure and coercive tied selling, appropriate products, remuneration and express consent, together with FCAC's Guideline on Appropriate Products and Services and its training expectations.
objectives: Recognise undue pressure, coercion, coercive tied selling and taking advantage of a person under section 627.04
Distinguish lawful preferential pricing (section 627.05) from coercive tied selling
Apply the appropriateness duty in section 627.06 using FCAC's know your consumer, know your product, assess and inform steps
Explain how remuneration must not interfere with appropriateness (section 627.07) and the training FCAC expects (paragraphs 17-18)
Apply the express consent rules in sections 627.08 and 627.09

cards.title: Stage two: the month-end push
cards.setting: Aurora Ridge Bank branch, Avenue du Mont-Royal, Montréal. 4:15 pm on the second-last day of the month.

lines.text: We're three credit cards short of the monthly target. The regional office has called twice.
At the counter, a student, Lucas, has come in to renew his line of credit. He looks tired and keeps checking his phone.
Our adviser told him the renewal 'goes faster' if he also takes the new travel card. He's hesitating.
Étienne, careful. That sounds like making one product a condition for another.
And a card a student may not need, sold under deadline pressure. Let's walk through what the Bank Act actually allows before anyone presses send.

cards.title: The fair-dealing rules in Division 2

scenes.heading: No false or misleading information
scenes.narration: Section 627.03 bans giving false or misleading information to a customer, the public or the Commissioner. That covers what staff say, not only what is printed.

scenes.heading: No undue pressure, coercion or taking advantage
scenes.narration: Section 627.04 bans undue pressure, coercion and taking advantage of a person. Undue pressure means pressure that could reasonably be considered excessive or persistent in the circumstances.

scenes.heading: No coercive tied selling
scenes.narration: The bank must not pressure or coerce someone to buy a product from the bank, an affiliate or anyone else as a condition for getting another product. A better price for a bundle is allowed under section 627.05.

scenes.heading: Appropriate products
scenes.narration: Section 627.06 requires policies and procedures so that products offered or sold to individuals for non-business purposes are appropriate to their circumstances, including their financial needs.

scenes.heading: Express consent first
scenes.narration: Section 627.08 says no product or service without the person's express consent and an agreement first. Using a product is not consent, and oral consent must be confirmed in writing without delay.

cards.title: Tied selling: lawful bundle or coercion?
cards.caption: The test: is the second product a reward or a condition imposed by pressure or coercion?

items.label: Pricing
items.left: Lower rate on a loan if the customer also opens an account
items.right: Loan refused unless the customer also buys insurance from an affiliate

items.label: Customer's choice
items.left: Customer can still get the loan at the normal price
items.right: Customer is told there is no loan without the second product

items.label: Security exception
items.left: Bank may require its approval of security, not unreasonably withheld
items.right: Bank insists on its own product when a suitable one exists elsewhere

cards.question: A customer is told: 'You can have this mortgage at our posted rate, or at a lower rate if you also move your chequing account to us.' The customer is free to take either option. How does the Bank Act treat this?
options: It is allowed: section 627.05 lets a bank offer more favourable terms on condition that the customer obtains another product
It is prohibited coercive tied selling under section 627.04
It is allowed only if FCAC approves each bundle in advance
It is allowed only for business customers, never for individuals
cards.explanation: Section 627.05 confirms that offering better terms on condition of buying another product is permitted. Section 627.04 targets undue pressure or coercion to obtain a product as a condition for another, which is different from a genuine choice.

cards.title: FCAC's appropriateness guideline in five steps
cards.body:
FCAC's **Guideline on Appropriate Products and Services** (in effect since 30 June 2022) explains section 627.06. A bank should:

1. **Know your consumer:** collect and assess information on the person's circumstances and financial needs.
2. **Know your product:** understand features, charges, risks and benefits, through an approval process across the product's life cycle.
3. **Assess appropriateness** when offering or selling, **even when the customer asked for the product**.
4. **Inform consumers** when a product was assessed as not appropriate, or the assessment could not be done, in clear, simple and not misleading language.
5. **Align remuneration** so pay, incentives and benefits do not interfere with appropriateness (section 627.07 and paragraphs 23-24).

The guideline adds that consumers are diverse and **some have financial vulnerabilities**, and that senior management and the responsible board committee should oversee the policies.

cards.title: Put the appropriateness journey in order
cards.prompt: Arrange the steps a bank follows under FCAC's guideline when a customer wants a product.
steps: Product passes the bank's internal assessment, review and approval process
Employee collects and verifies the customer's circumstances and financial needs
Employee assesses whether the product is appropriate for this customer
If it is not appropriate, employee tells the customer clearly so they can decide
Bank keeps records showing the assessment was done and its outcome

cards.title: A turn: the outbound sales unit
cards.setting: Mei's desk, Vancouver, by video call.

lines.text: I found an FCAC decision that worries me. Decision 142, Scotiabank, posted December 2021.
The outbound sales unit. Customers received credit cards, lines of credit or optional insurance without express consent.
FCAC staff listed the causes: inadequate procedures, lack of training, inappropriate incentive programs and unclear roles.
So training and incentives were part of the root cause, not just bad luck on one team.
Exactly. And that is why the framework now ties training (627.02), appropriateness (627.06) and remuneration (627.07) together.

cards.title: Real case: Scotiabank, consent and an outbound sales unit (2021)
cards.body:
In **Decision #142** (posted December 2021), FCAC staff alleged that **the Bank of Nova Scotia** breached the **Negative Option Billing Regulations**, the pre-framework consent rule, by providing credit cards, lines of credit or optional insurance without customers' **express consent**.

- Staff proposed an **$80,000** penalty and said the control deficiencies included **inadequate policies and procedures, lack of training, inappropriate incentive programs** and unclear roles, which weakened senior management oversight.
- The Commissioner found a violation from **February to June 2018**, when the unit was closed. Because of the shorter period and other mitigating factors, the Commissioner imposed **no penalty**, but decided to name the bank.

**Lesson:** sales incentives, training and clear roles are part of consent compliance. Today, sections 627.02, 627.07 and 627.08 of the Bank Act deal with them directly.

cards.title: Lucas and the travel card
cards.situation: Back in Montréal. The adviser tells Étienne that Lucas, a full-time student with a part-time job, now says he will 'take the card if it gets the line of credit renewed today'. The renewal does not depend on the card. The card has an annual fee and Lucas mentioned he never travels. The adviser is two cards short of a bonus threshold.

choices.text: Stop the card sale: tell Lucas plainly that the renewal does not depend on the card, finish the renewal, and only discuss the card if he raises it and it suits his needs.
choices.outcome: Best choice. It removes the coercive link (section 627.04), avoids a product that looks inappropriate for his circumstances (section 627.06), and puts the customer ahead of the bonus (section 627.07).

choices.text: Sell the card but waive the first year's fee so Lucas is not harmed.
choices.outcome: Partly right on harm but wrong on the law. Lucas still thinks the card is a condition of renewal, and a product that does not meet his needs remains inappropriate.

choices.text: Sell the card: Lucas agreed, and his signature is express consent.
choices.outcome: Poor. Consent obtained by implying a condition that does not exist is tainted by undue pressure and misleading information, and the appropriateness duty still applies.

choices.text: Let the adviser decide; it's his customer and his target.
choices.outcome: Poor. The manager has a duty to stop conduct that breaches the bank's policies. Incentives that drive such sales are exactly what section 627.07 targets.

cards.title: Is the sale safe? Need and pressure
cards.caption: Appropriateness and freedom from pressure are separate tests. A sale must pass both.

items.label: Fits needs, pressured
items.detail: Still a breach risk: pressure or coercion is banned even for a suitable product

items.label: Fits needs, free choice
items.detail: The target: appropriate product, express consent, no pressure

items.label: Poor fit, pressured
items.detail: Highest risk: likely inappropriate and undue pressure; stop the sale

items.label: Poor fit, free choice
items.detail: Inform the customer it is not appropriate; follow policy if they still want it

cards.title: Consent facts every seller needs

cards.front: Is using a product the same as consenting to it?
cards.back: No. Section 627.08(3) says use of a product or service is not express consent.

cards.front: What if the customer agrees by phone?
cards.back: Oral consent is allowed, but the bank must send written confirmation of that consent without delay.

cards.front: What comes before providing an ongoing product?
cards.back: Express consent, an agreement, and a copy of the agreement for products provided on an ongoing basis.

cards.front: How must the request for consent be worded?
cards.back: In a manner and language that is clear, simple and not misleading (section 627.09).

cards.front: Can the bank charge a fee the customer never agreed to?
cards.back: No. Section 627.12 requires express consent, an agreement providing for the charge and proper disclosure.

cards.front: What if a charge was imposed without consent?
cards.back: Division 4 (section 627.997) requires the bank to credit or refund it.

cards.question: Under FCAC's Guideline on Appropriate Products and Services, what training should a bank require for people who offer or sell its products?
options: Initial and ongoing training on the bank's appropriateness obligations and on the features, charges, risks and benefits of the products they sell
A single induction module on general banking history, with no refresher
Training only for staff who sell investment products, not deposits or credit
Training only after a customer has complained about a sale
cards.explanation: Paragraphs 17-18 expect initial and ongoing training covering the bank's appropriateness obligations and the products sold, including how to explain them, with the bank monitoring completion and regularly reviewing and updating the training.

cards.title: Real case: RBC, credit limit increases and training material (2021)
cards.body:
In **Decision #139** (posted February 2021), the FCAC Commissioner found that the **Royal Bank of Canada** failed to obtain cardholders' **express consent** before applying **pre-approved credit card limit increases** between 2015 and 2017, under the regulations in force at the time, and imposed a **$350,000** penalty.

- RBC argued **due diligence** and pointed to its phone-channel training manual.
- The Commissioner found the defence unproven. Reviewing the **training material**, call recordings and other documents, the decision found the bank had **not consistently presented consent as a regulatory requirement** in both sales channels and had **not clearly set out how employees were to show** they had obtained it.

**Lesson:** to rely on training as a defence, it must teach the actual legal requirement and the exact steps staff take to meet it, in every channel.

cards.title: Stage two take-aways
items: Sections 627.03 and 627.04 ban misleading information, undue pressure, coercion (including coercive tied selling) and taking advantage of a person.
Section 627.05 allows genuine bundled pricing; coercion makes a bundle unlawful.
Section 627.06 requires appropriateness policies; FCAC expects know your consumer, know your product, assessment, informing and aligned remuneration.
FCAC expects initial and ongoing training for anyone who offers or sells bank products, with completion monitored and content reviewed (paragraphs 17-18).
Express consent and an agreement must come first; use is not consent, and oral consent needs prompt written confirmation.

cards.prompt: Think of the last product you recommended. What did you know about the customer's needs, and could anything you said have sounded like a condition or a deadline?

quiz.question: How does Part XII.2 of the Bank Act define undue pressure?
options: Any mention of a product the customer did not ask about during a meeting at the branch
Any sales call made outside business hours or more than once in the same calendar month
Pressure that could reasonably be seen as excessive or persistent in the circumstances
Pressure that causes the customer a proven financial loss confirmed by an external body
quiz.explanation: Section 627.01 defines undue pressure as pressure, through a practice, communication or otherwise, that could reasonably be considered excessive or persistent in the circumstances. No financial loss is needed.

quiz.question: An adviser tells a customer: 'We can only approve your car loan if you also buy creditor insurance from our affiliate.' The customer could easily get equivalent cover elsewhere. Which provision is most directly breached?
options: Section 627.13, the low-balance alert rule
Section 627.04, the ban on coercive tied selling
Section 627.47, annual complaint information
Section 979.3, whistleblowing procedures
quiz.explanation: Imposing pressure or coercion to obtain a product from a particular person, including an affiliate, as a condition for another product is prohibited by section 627.04(a).

quiz.question: A customer gets a lower mortgage rate because she also opens a chequing account, and she was offered the mortgage at the regular rate too. Why is this lawful?
options: Section 627.05 allows better terms on condition of buying another product
FCAC has granted all banks a blanket exemption from the tied selling rule for mortgages
Mortgages are outside Part XII.2 altogether, so no consumer provision applies to them
Bundling is only illegal when the second product comes from a third party, not the bank
quiz.explanation: Section 627.05 confirms that preferential terms tied to another product are allowed. What is banned is undue pressure or coercion to obtain a product as a condition for another.

quiz.question: According to FCAC's appropriateness guideline, when should a bank assess whether a product is appropriate?
options: Only when the bank itself recommends the product
When it offers or sells a product, even when the customer asked for it
Only for credit products above a set dollar amount
Only after the customer has complained
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 19 expects an appropriateness assessment whenever the bank offers or sells products, including those requested by consumers.

quiz.question: Mei designs a bonus that pays advisers per credit card sold, with no check on whether cards suit customers. Which Bank Act section is most at risk?
options: Section 627.993, which requires written notice to customers before closing a branch
Section 627.44, which sets the contents of the complaint record and its retention period
Section 627.07, on remuneration that must not undermine appropriateness
Section 627.19, which requires a written statement when the bank refuses to open an account
quiz.explanation: Section 627.07 requires the bank to ensure remuneration and benefits do not interfere with staff's ability to follow appropriateness policies. FCAC also expects remuneration metrics to align with appropriateness (paragraph 23).

quiz.question: A customer agrees by phone to add overdraft protection to her account. What must the bank do under section 627.08?
options: Provide written confirmation of her oral consent without delay
Nothing more, because oral consent is not permitted at all
Wait 30 days before activating, then send a survey
Ask her to visit a branch to sign before any confirmation is sent
quiz.explanation: Section 627.08(2) allows oral consent but requires the bank to give written confirmation of it without delay.

quiz.question: A customer used a credit card that arrived in the mail without his request. The bank says his use proves he consented. Is that right?
options: Yes. Activation and use are a valid form of express consent
No. Use of a product is not express consent under section 627.08(3)
Yes, provided the card's annual fee is below a set amount
No, but only because cards may never be mailed to customers
quiz.explanation: Section 627.08(3) says use of the product or service does not constitute express consent. The bank needed express consent and an agreement first.

quiz.question: Under FCAC's appropriateness guideline, what should happen when a bank assesses a product as not appropriate for a customer who still wants it?
options: The bank must sell it anyway, since the customer has the final say
The bank must report the customer to FCAC
The bank informs the customer clearly and follows its policy on how to proceed
The bank must close all of the customer's accounts
quiz.explanation: Paragraphs 21-22 expect policies on how to proceed when a customer wants a product assessed as not appropriate, and clear, simple, not misleading information so the customer can make an informed decision.

quiz.question: In Decision #142 about Scotiabank's outbound sales unit, which control deficiencies did FCAC staff identify?
options: A cyber breach that exposed customer passwords and card numbers to criminals
Mortgage rates that were set too high compared with the rest of the market
Failure to file suspicious transaction reports with FINTRAC on time
Weak procedures, lack of training, poor incentives and unclear roles
quiz.explanation: FCAC staff linked the lack of express consent to inadequate policies and procedures, lack of training, inappropriate incentive programs and unclear roles and responsibilities.

quiz.question: In Decision #139, why did RBC's due diligence defence fail?
options: RBC did not have any training manual or written sales procedure of any kind for credit cards
Its training and procedures did not clearly teach consent as a legal requirement
Due diligence is never available as a defence in proceedings under the FCAC Act
RBC raised the defence after the 30-day period for representations had already passed
quiz.explanation: Due diligence is a defence under the FCAC Act, but the Commissioner found RBC's evidence insufficient: training materials and procedures did not consistently treat consent as a regulatory requirement or set out how employees should demonstrate it.

sessions.title: Disclosure, access to basic banking and the coming fraud duty
sessions.summary: Apply the disclosure rules in Division 3 of Part XII.2, the right to open a retail deposit account and the limited grounds for refusal, branch closure notices, and the new consumer-targeted fraud duty in section 627.134, which is NOT YET IN FORCE.
objectives: Apply the clear, simple and not misleading standard to disclosures, advertisements and consent requests
Open or refuse a retail deposit account in line with sections 627.17 to 627.19
Describe low-balance alerts, renewal notices and branch closure notice periods
Explain what section 627.134 will require on consumer-targeted fraud, including initial and recurrent training, and that it is not yet in force
Draw lessons from FCAC penalties for inaccurate statements and disclosures

cards.title: Stage three: the man with two documents
cards.setting: Aurora Ridge Bank branch, North Main Street, Winnipeg. 10:05 am.

lines.text: Kevin Morningstar, contact centre and fraud operations, Winnipeg. I'm covering the branch floor this morning.
A man named Daniel asks to open a basic chequing account. He has a provincial health card and a recent utility bill, no credit history and $20 in cash.
The new teller whispers: 'We usually need a minimum deposit, and he's just come out of bankruptcy. Can we say no?'
On a video call: Kevin, the Bank Act gives people a right to a retail deposit account. The grounds to refuse are narrow, and bankruptcy alone isn't one of them.
Then I need my team to know the rules cold. And I keep hearing about a new fraud training duty. Is that in force?
Not yet. Let's sort what applies today from what's coming.

cards.title: Disclosure that customers can actually use

scenes.heading: Clear, simple, not misleading
scenes.narration: When Division 3 requires disclosure, section 627.55 says it must be clear, simple and not misleading, and in writing unless the Division says otherwise.

scenes.heading: The information box
scenes.narration: For some products, key information must sit in one prominent information box on the application or before the agreement. On phone sales, staff must point it out orally.

scenes.heading: Advertising
scenes.narration: Section 627.14 requires every advertisement in Canada to be accurate, clear and not misleading. A footnote cannot fix a misleading headline.

scenes.heading: Alerts and renewals
scenes.narration: Banks must send electronic alerts when a personal account balance or available credit falls below a set amount, $100 by default, unless the customer opts out. Renewal notices come before a term ends.

scenes.heading: Branch closures
scenes.narration: Before closing a retail deposit-taking branch, the bank must give FCAC, customers and the public written notice: four months, or six months in a rural area with no other branch within 10 km.

cards.title: Opening a retail deposit account under section 627.17
cards.caption: The duty applies to member banks (CDIC members). A refusal must be in writing with complaint information (section 627.19).

items.label: Request in person
items.detail: Natural person asks at a branch or point of service that opens retail deposit accounts

items.label: Identification
items.detail: Two documents from a reliable source, or one plus confirmation by a customer or person of good standing

items.label: Consent to checks
items.detail: If asked, the person consents to verification of documents and refusal grounds

items.label: Photo ID if doubt
items.detail: If identity misrepresentation is reasonably suspected, government photo ID with signature

items.label: Open with no minimum
items.detail: No initial minimum deposit or minimum balance may be required

cards.title: Valid ground to refuse a retail deposit account?
cards.prompt: Decide whether each reason can justify refusing Daniel's request under section 627.18.

items.text: Reasonable grounds to believe the account will be used for fraud
A history of fraud against financial service providers within the past seven years
Reasonable grounds to believe he knowingly made a material misrepresentation to open it
Refusal is needed to protect staff or customers from physical harm or harassment
He has been bankrupt, with no evidence of fraud
He cannot make an opening deposit of $100
He is unemployed and has no credit history

cards.question: Aurora Ridge Bank decides not to open an account for a person who meets one of the refusal grounds. What does section 627.19 require?
options: A written statement that the account will not be opened, plus information on the bank's complaint process and how to contact FCAC and the external complaints body
An oral explanation only, so that no record exists
A report to FINTRAC in every case of refusal
Nothing: refusals need no explanation
cards.explanation: Section 627.19 requires a written statement that the bank will not open the account and the information referred to in section 627.65(a) to (c), which covers how to complain and whom to contact.

cards.title: Bankruptcy is not a red flag on its own
cards.body:
Section 627.18(2) is explicit: the fact that a person **is or has been bankrupt** does not, without evidence of fraud or other illegal activity linked to the bankruptcy, give reasonable grounds to believe the account will be used for illegal or fraudulent purposes.

Train tellers to separate **credit risk** (relevant for loans) from **access to a basic account** (a right, with narrow exceptions). If in doubt, escalate to a supervisor rather than turning the person away.

cards.title: A turn: credits that never moved
cards.setting: Kevin's fraud operations room, Winnipeg. Afternoon.

lines.text: When a customer reports card fraud, we close the card and open a new account. FCAC fined RBC $4.25 million over that exact process.
Summary of proceeding 5, posted June 2026. Credits on the old account were not moved to the new one, so statements were wrong.
And CIBC was fined $3 million in 2023 for a very similar problem with deactivated cards.
Fraud processes are disclosure processes too. Every statement after a fraud claim must still be accurate.
So when the new fraud duty arrives, our training must cover both: stopping fraud and getting the follow-up right.

cards.title: Real cases: statements after fraud at RBC (2026) and CIBC (2023)
cards.body:
**RBC.** FCAC's **Summary of proceeding #5** (posted June 2026) reports that the **Royal Bank of Canada** paid a **$4.25 million** penalty on 17 April 2026 for one violation of its **Bank Act disclosure obligations** on monthly credit card statements. From 2001 to 2024, when a card account was deactivated and moved to a new account after fraud was reported, certain credits were not transferred. About **227,947 accounts** were affected and RBC transferred and refunded about **$22.4 million**. FCAC cited inadequate control and oversight procedures.

**CIBC.** In **Decision #144** (posted June 2023), the Commissioner found that the **Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce** violated the Cost of Borrowing (Banks) Regulations by not carrying some transactions to the new statement after a lost, stolen or defrauded card was deactivated, and imposed a **$3.0 million** penalty.

**Lesson:** customer remedies after fraud must flow through to accurate statements.

cards.title: Section 627.134: consumer-targeted fraud (NOT YET IN FORCE)
cards.body:
Amendments made by the **Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1** (S.C. 2026, c. 3, s. 334) add section 627.134 to the Bank Act. The official consolidation lists it under **amendments not in force**: it applies only from a date to be fixed. Once in force, a bank must:

- **Adopt and follow policies and procedures** to detect and prevent consumer-targeted fraud and mitigate its impacts.
- Set out **criteria** for when a transaction is suspicious; when to suspend, cancel or otherwise act on it; whether a person is a victim and a remedy is available; and what remedies exist, plus how each decision is communicated.
- Give **initial and recurrent training** on detecting and preventing consumer-targeted fraud and on these policies to **employees, representatives, agents and other intermediaries who deal with customers in Canada**.
- Send FCAC an **annual report** on consumer-targeted fraud.

The new definition covers transactions that are **unauthorized**, or **authorized as a result of coercion or deception**, such as a scam.

cards.title: The pre-emptive fraud module
cards.situation: Kevin wants to launch a consumer-targeted fraud module next month for contact centre and branch staff, covering scams where customers are tricked into authorising payments. His director asks whether the bank should state in its board report that it 'now complies with section 627.134 of the Bank Act'.

choices.text: Launch the module as good practice under existing risk management, but describe section 627.134 accurately: enacted, not yet in force, and coming into force on a date still to be fixed.
choices.outcome: Best choice. Early training helps customers now and prepares for the duty, and the board receives an accurate picture of the law's status.

choices.text: Delay all fraud training until the government fixes the coming-into-force date.
choices.outcome: Partly defensible on legal grounds, but it leaves staff unprepared for scams that already harm customers and makes the eventual rollout rushed.

choices.text: Tell the board the bank is now compliant with section 627.134 in force.
choices.outcome: Poor. The section is not in force, so stating compliance with it as current law is inaccurate, and the content of required criteria may still be set by regulation.

choices.text: Tell staff the section is in force so they take the module seriously.
choices.outcome: Poor. Giving staff false information about the law undermines trust and accuracy. Motivate the training with real customer harm instead.

cards.title: From framework to fraud duty
cards.caption: Check the current status on the Justice Laws Website before you describe a provision as in force.

items.label: Framework in force
items.detail: Part XII.2 and the Framework Regulations apply to banks

items.label: Fraud duty enacted
items.detail: Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 adds sections 627.131 to 627.135

items.label: Revised complaint guideline
items.detail: FCAC's revised complaint-handling guideline takes effect

items.label: Fraud duty in force
items.detail: Section 627.134 applies only once brought into force

cards.title: Match the disclosure rule to the situation
cards.prompt: Link each Bank Act rule to the situation it governs.

pairs.right: A billboard advertising a savings rate must be accurate, clear and not misleading
An electronic alert when a personal account balance drops below the threshold
Key cost information shown in a single prominent information box
Written notice before closing a retail deposit-taking branch
Required disclosure must be clear, simple, not misleading and generally in writing

cards.question: Which statement about section 627.134 of the Bank Act (consumer-targeted fraud) is accurate as of November 2026?
options: It has been enacted but is not yet in force; it will apply from a date to be fixed
It has been in force since 30 June 2022 as part of the original framework
It is only an FCAC consultation paper with no legal text
It applies only to credit unions regulated by provinces
cards.explanation: Section 627.134 was added by the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 and appears among the amendments not in force in the official consolidation. It was not part of the 2022 framework.

cards.title: Stage three take-aways
items: Required disclosure must be clear, simple and not misleading; advertisements must be accurate, clear and not misleading.
Member banks must open retail deposit accounts for eligible individuals without a minimum deposit or balance; refusal grounds are narrow and must be explained in writing.
Bankruptcy alone, with no evidence of fraud, is not a ground to refuse an account.
Branch closures need written notice: four months, or six months in rural areas with no other branch within 10 km.
Section 627.134 will require fraud policies, initial and recurrent training and annual reporting, but it is NOT YET IN FORCE.

cards.prompt: When you explain a fee, rate or refusal to a customer, what do you do to check they understood it? What would make your explanation clearer?

quiz.question: What standard does section 627.55 set for disclosure required under Division 3?
options: Clear, simple and not misleading, and in writing unless the Division provides otherwise
Brief enough to fit on one page, in any format
Approved in advance by FCAC for every product
Provided orally, with a written copy only on request
quiz.explanation: Section 627.55(1) requires disclosure in a manner and language that is clear, simple and not misleading, and in writing unless Division 3 provides otherwise.

quiz.question: A person asks to open a retail deposit account at a member bank branch, presenting two acceptable documents. The teller asks for a $50 minimum opening deposit. Is that allowed?
options: No. Section 627.17(4) bars requiring an initial minimum deposit or a minimum balance
Yes, a minimum of up to $100 is allowed for new customers
Yes, if the branch posts the requirement prominently
No, but only if the person is receiving government benefits
quiz.explanation: Section 627.17(4) prohibits requiring an initial minimum deposit or the maintenance of a minimum balance for such accounts.

quiz.question: Which of these is a valid ground under section 627.18 for refusing to open a retail deposit account?
options: The person has no credit history in Canada and cannot show a regular income
The person was bankrupt two years ago, with no evidence of fraud or other illegal activity
The person lives in a different province from the branch where the request is made
Grounds to believe the person knowingly made a material misrepresentation
quiz.explanation: Section 627.18(1)(c) covers knowing material misrepresentation. Lack of credit history and residence are not grounds, and section 627.18(2) says bankruptcy alone is not evidence of illegal or fraudulent purpose.

quiz.question: A person who wants to open an account has only one document showing name and date of birth. Under section 627.17, how can the bank still open the account?
options: Only if the person deposits at least $1,000 to show the account will be actively used
Only after FCAC confirms the person's identity through its Consumer Information Centre
If a customer or community member of good standing confirms the identity
It cannot; two documents from a reliable source are always required, with no alternative
quiz.explanation: Section 627.17(1)(a)(ii) allows one reliable document showing name and date of birth if identity is also confirmed by a customer in good standing with the bank or a person of good standing in the community.

quiz.question: Aurora Ridge Bank plans to close its only branch in a rural Saskatchewan town; the nearest other branch is 40 km away. What notice must it give customers and the public?
options: Written notice at least 30 days before closure, posted at the branch and on the website
Written notice at least six months ahead, including to the local mayor
Notice at least four months before closure, by email only, with no notice to local officials
No notice, as long as online and telephone banking remain available to all customers
quiz.explanation: Section 627.993(1)(c) requires six months' written notice to customers, the public and the local government head when the branch is rural with no other retail deposit-taking branch within 10 km.

quiz.question: Unless the customer sets another amount or opts out, at what level does section 627.13 require an electronic low-balance alert on a personal deposit account (absent a prescribed amount)?
quiz.explanation: Section 627.13(1) requires an alert when the balance falls below the amount the person sets, or the prescribed amount, or, if none is prescribed, $100.

quiz.question: Under the coming section 627.134, which group will have to receive initial and recurrent consumer-targeted fraud training?
options: Only members of the board of directors and the bank's senior executive team
Only staff in the fraud investigations unit who review suspicious transactions
Employees, agents and intermediaries who deal with customers in Canada
Only customers who report a fraud, through materials the bank sends after the claim
quiz.explanation: Section 627.134(3), once in force, requires training for employees, representatives, agents or mandataries and other intermediaries who deal with customers who are in Canada.

quiz.question: How does the amended Bank Act define consumer-targeted fraud (in the provisions not yet in force)?
options: Only transactions made with a stolen physical card
Only frauds above an amount set by FCAC each year
Only frauds committed by bank employees against customers
It includes transactions that are unauthorized or authorized as a result of coercion or deception
quiz.explanation: The new definition in section 627.01(1) covers transactions that are unauthorized or that are authorized as a result of coercion or deception, so authorised push-payment scams are included.

quiz.question: In FCAC's 2026 summary of proceeding about RBC, what went wrong?
options: Credits were not moved to new card accounts after fraud, so statements were wrong
RBC refused to open basic accounts for newcomers to Canada who presented foreign passports
RBC charged customers a fee when it closed branches in rural areas without proper notice
RBC retaliated against employees who reported wrongdoing in its card fraud operations
quiz.explanation: FCAC found a violation of RBC's Bank Act disclosure obligations: after fraud-related account migrations, some credits were not carried over, producing inaccurate monthly statements and extra charges for some customers.

quiz.question: Kevin's director wants to write that Aurora Ridge Bank 'complies with section 627.134 as currently in force'. What is the accurate position?
options: The statement is accurate because the section took effect on assent
The statement is accurate because FCAC guidelines made it binding in 2024
The section was repealed, so the board report should not mention fraud
The section is enacted but not yet in force, so the bank can only describe its preparations
quiz.explanation: Section 627.134 appears among the amendments not in force; it applies from a date to be fixed. The bank can describe voluntary training and readiness, not compliance with a provision in force.

sessions.title: Complaints, the external complaints body and whistleblowing
sessions.summary: Handle complaints under sections 627.43 to 627.54 and the 56-day period, explain escalation to the Ombudsman for Banking Services and Investments, apply FCAC's complaint-handling training expectations (current and revised guideline), and use the Bank Act whistleblowing protections in sections 979.1 to 979.4.
objectives: Recognise a complaint as defined in the Bank Act and start the 56-day clock correctly
Describe the bank's complaint duties: procedures, designated employees, acknowledgement, records, reporting and public information
Explain when and how a customer can go to the external complaints body (OBSI) and what OBSI must do
Apply FCAC's expectations for complaint-handling training, including the changes in the guideline revised in June 2026
Apply the whistleblowing rules: what wrongdoing is, where employees can report, confidentiality and the ban on retaliation

cards.title: Stage four: 'This isn't a complaint, is it?'
cards.setting: Complaints office, Aurora Ridge Bank, Mississauga. 9:20 am.

lines.text: Priya Raman, complaints lead and our senior designated employee. Listen to this call note from yesterday.
A customer told a contact centre agent she was 'really annoyed' that her mortgage payment changed without warning. The agent explained the change and logged it as an 'enquiry'.
She didn't say the word 'complaint'. Isn't an enquiry fine?
The Bank Act defines a complaint as dissatisfaction, whether justified or not, about a product or service or how it was provided. No magic word needed.
And the 56-day period started when she first told us. If we mislabel it, we miss the clock, the record and the report to FCAC.
So the agent needs training, not blame. Let's map the whole path.

cards.title: The complaint journey under the Bank Act

scenes.heading: Recognise it
scenes.narration: A complaint is any expressed dissatisfaction, justified or not, about a product or service or how it was offered, sold or provided. Any channel counts.

scenes.heading: Acknowledge and record
scenes.narration: The bank gives the person a written acknowledgement of the date it received the complaint, and keeps a record with the details the Act lists for at least seven years.

scenes.heading: Deal with it within 56 days
scenes.narration: The Framework Regulations set 56 days after the day the complaint is received as the period for dealing with it. Designated employees handle complaints that cannot be settled at first contact.

scenes.heading: Escalate to OBSI
scenes.narration: If the customer is not satisfied, or 56 days pass, they can go to the external complaints body. FCAC's consumer pages name it as the Ombudsman for Banking Services and Investments, OBSI.

scenes.heading: Report and learn
scenes.narration: The bank reports complaints to FCAC quarterly, publishes annual complaint information and analyses data to find systemic issues.

cards.title: Key complaint deadlines
cards.caption: Figures from Bank Act sections 627.44 to 627.49 and section 14 of the Framework Regulations.

items.label: Bank deals with complaint
items.detail: From the day the complaint is received (Framework Regulations, s. 14)

items.label: OBSI out-of-scope reasons
items.detail: Written reasons if a complaint is outside its terms of reference

items.label: Quarterly report to FCAC
items.detail: After each quarter, records of complaints handled by designated employees

items.label: OBSI final recommendation
items.detail: After OBSI has all the information it needs

items.label: Annual public information
items.detail: After financial year end, on the bank's websites

items.label: Complaint record kept
items.detail: Minimum retention under section 627.44

cards.question: A customer tells a teller on 3 March that she is unhappy her account fee went up. On what day does the 56-day period start?
options: When the bank received the complaint, here 3 March, whatever the channel
When she puts the complaint in writing
When a designated employee first reviews the file
When the bank sends its written acknowledgement
cards.explanation: Section 14 of the Framework Regulations sets the period as 56 days after the day the complaint is received. FCAC's revised guideline adds that the clock starts on first communication by any channel and is not paused.

cards.title: What the bank must have in place
cards.body:
Sections 627.43 to 627.47 require the bank to:

- **Set up complaint procedures** satisfactory to the Commissioner, **file them with FCAC** and keep them updated.
- **Designate** one officer or employee in Canada to implement the procedures, and one or more to **receive and deal with** complaints.
- **Avoid misleading names:** no term suggesting the internal process is independent, such as **'ombudsman'**.
- Give the complainant a **written acknowledgement** of the date received, plus information on its procedures, the external complaints body and FCAC.
- Keep a **record** of each complaint for at least **seven years**, accessible to FCAC.
- **Report** complaints handled by designated employees to FCAC within **60 days** after each quarter.
- Publish annual information on complaints handled by its most senior designated employee within **135 days** after year end.

Every bank must be a **member of the external complaints body** and give it all relevant information **without delay** when notified of a complaint.

cards.title: Put a complaint's path in order
cards.prompt: Arrange the steps Aurora Ridge Bank follows for a complaint that is not resolved at first contact.
steps: Employee recognises the customer's dissatisfaction as a complaint and logs it
Bank sends a written acknowledgement with the date received and process information
Complaint is referred to a designated employee who investigates
Bank gives its final written response within the 56-day period
Customer who is still unhappy takes the complaint to OBSI
Bank gives OBSI all relevant information without delay

cards.title: Training on complaints: today and from June 2027
cards.body:
FCAC's **Guideline on Complaint-Handling Procedures** expects:

- **Initial and ongoing formal training** for all employees who deal with complaints.
- A **system to monitor** training status and ways to **measure and test** whether training works.
- **Regular review and timely updates**, especially when laws or internal procedures change.
- **Role-specific** training for designated employees.

The current version applies until **22 June 2027** (training at paragraphs 18-19). FCAC published a **revised guideline in June 2026, effective 23 June 2027** (training at paragraphs 19-21). The revision adds, among other things:

- Referral to a designated employee within **14 calendar days** to be timely.
- The 56-day period is **not paused for any reason**.
- A written **Notice of Final Decision** that tells the customer about OBSI.
- Stronger expectations on **systemic issues, redress and remediation**.

cards.title: Complaint or not?
cards.prompt: Under the Bank Act definition, sort each customer statement.

items.text: 'I'm fed up that your app charged me twice.'
'The adviser pushed a card on me that I didn't want.'
'Honestly, I think your new fee is unfair, even if it's in the contract.'
'It took three visits to get my address changed. Not impressed.'
'What are your branch hours on Saturday?'
'Can you send me a copy of last month's statement?'
'Please increase my e-transfer limit for a house deposit.'

cards.title: A turn: the employee who spotted the pattern
cards.setting: A quiet meeting room, Toronto. Late afternoon.

lines.text: A teller in Halifax emails Nadia privately. She has seen a colleague open overdraft protection on elderly customers' accounts without asking them.
She's worried her manager will find out she reported it. The manager is the colleague's friend.
Can she go straight to FCAC instead of us?
Yes. Section 979.2 lets an employee report to the bank, to the FCAC Commissioner, to OSFI, to another financial regulator or to law enforcement. And her identity must be kept confidential.
And if her manager punishes her?
Section 979.4 bans dismissing, suspending, demoting, disciplining, harassing or otherwise disadvantaging her for a report made on reasonable belief.

cards.title: Whistleblowing under Part XVI.1 of the Bank Act
cards.caption: FCAC's whistleblowing guideline also expects anonymous reporting to be possible and regular training for all employees.

items.label: Wrongdoing
items.detail: Breach of the Act or regulations, a bank code or public commitment, or a bank policy (s. 979.1)

items.label: Report
items.detail: To the bank, FCAC Commissioner, OSFI, another regulator or law enforcement (s. 979.2(1))

items.label: Confidentiality
items.detail: Identity protected; limited disclosure for investigations, with the employee informed (s. 979.2)

items.label: Procedures
items.detail: Bank must establish and implement procedures to deal with reports (s. 979.3)

items.label: No retaliation
items.detail: No dismissal, demotion, discipline, harassment or other disadvantage (s. 979.4)

cards.title: The Halifax teller's report
cards.situation: The teller from Halifax tells you she wants to report anonymously, through the bank's whistleblowing hotline, that a colleague added overdraft protection to elderly customers' accounts without consent. Her branch manager, who is close to the colleague, asks you who made the report 'so I can sort it out at branch level'.

choices.text: Decline to reveal anything that could identify her, handle the report through the bank's whistleblowing procedures, and record it so any consumer breach is assessed for reporting to FCAC.
choices.outcome: Best choice. Section 979.2 requires confidentiality, section 979.3 requires the bank to deal with reports through its procedures, and FCAC's guideline expects consumer breaches found this way to be assessed for reporting.

choices.text: Tell the manager in confidence, since managers need to know to fix problems.
choices.outcome: Poor. Disclosure to the manager is not one of the permitted exceptions and exposes her to the retaliation that section 979.4 prohibits.

choices.text: Ask the teller to raise it with her manager first, as a courtesy.
choices.outcome: Poor. Employees may report directly to the bank's channel or to regulators; sending her back to a conflicted manager undermines the process.

choices.text: Treat it as a customer complaint and pass it to the complaints team without telling her.
choices.outcome: Partly right: affected customers may need redress. But a staff report of wrongdoing must also go through whistleblowing procedures with its confidentiality safeguards.

cards.title: Whistleblowing myths and facts

cards.back: Fact: it also covers breaches of the Bank Act or regulations, of a voluntary code or public commitment, and of the bank's own policies or procedures.

cards.front: Myth: staff must report internally first.
cards.back: Fact: an employee may report to the bank or directly to the FCAC Commissioner, OSFI, another financial regulator or law enforcement.

cards.front: Myth: a report must be signed.
cards.back: Fact: FCAC's guideline expects the bank's procedures to allow anonymous reports.

cards.front: Myth: only compliance staff need whistleblowing training.
cards.back: Fact: FCAC expects regular, ongoing training for all employees, plus tailored training for those who handle reports.

cards.front: Myth: protection depends on the report being proven.
cards.back: Fact: section 979.4 protects employees who acted on reasonable belief.

cards.question: Which statement about the external complaints body is correct?
options: Every bank must be a member, and the body must give a final written recommendation within 120 days of having all the information it needs
Membership is voluntary, and the body may charge customers a filing fee
FCAC itself acts as the external complaints body and resolves each complaint
Customers can only go to it after a court has ruled on their case
cards.explanation: Section 627.48(3) makes membership mandatory and section 627.49 requires free services to complainants and a final recommendation within 120 days. FCAC says it does not resolve individual complaints.

cards.title: Real case: 500 complaints as an early warning (BMO, 2025)
cards.body:
Revisit FCAC's **Summary of proceeding #4**. When setting BMO's **$4 million** penalty for inaccurate fee waiver disclosures, FCAC pointed to BMO's negligence in failing to put in place adequate controls and effective monitoring **despite over 500 customer complaints** about the monthly plan fees.

What this means for complaint handlers:

- A complaint is often the **first sign of a systemic issue**. Both versions of FCAC's guideline expect banks to analyse complaint data, and the revised one expects banks to look for **root causes** that may affect other customers.
- Front-line staff who resolve each complaint one by one, with a refund and an apology, may fix the symptom while the **root cause keeps harming** thousands of others.
- Training should show staff **how to flag** repeated complaints on the same issue.

**Lesson:** handle the individual complaint and feed the pattern into the bank's systemic issue process.

cards.title: Stage four take-aways
items: A complaint is any expressed dissatisfaction, justified or not; no special words or channel are needed.
Banks must deal with complaints within 56 days, acknowledge them in writing, keep records for seven years, report quarterly to FCAC and publish annual information.
Customers can escalate to the external complaints body, OBSI, which is free; every bank must be a member and share information without delay.
FCAC expects initial and ongoing formal complaint-handling training with monitoring and testing; the revised guideline takes effect on 23 June 2027.
Employees may report wrongdoing internally or to FCAC, OSFI, other regulators or police; identity is confidential and retaliation is banned.

cards.prompt: Think of the last time a customer sounded unhappy with you. Did you treat it as a complaint? What would you do differently with the 56-day clock in mind?

quiz.question: How does the Bank Act define a complaint?
options: Any written letter addressed to the bank's president or board about a product
A grievance a customer files with FCAC that FCAC accepts after its own review of the facts
Dissatisfaction, justified or not, about a product or service or how it was provided
Dissatisfaction that the bank, after investigating, agrees is justified and must be remedied
quiz.explanation: Section 627.01 defines a complaint broadly as dissatisfaction, justified or not, expressed to an institution about a product or service or the way it is offered, sold or provided.

quiz.question: What period do the Framework Regulations prescribe for a bank to deal with a complaint?
options: 30 days after the bank acknowledges it
56 days after the day the complaint is received
90 days after the customer puts it in writing
120 days after the complaint is escalated internally
quiz.explanation: Section 14 of the Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations sets 56 days after the day on which the complaint is received.

quiz.question: Aurora Ridge Bank wants to call its senior internal complaints unit the 'Customer Ombudsman Office'. What does the Bank Act say?
options: It may, as long as the unit reports directly to the board rather than to management
It may, provided FCAC approves the name when the bank files its complaint procedures
It must, because the Act requires every bank to have an internal ombudsman office
It may not use 'ombudsman' or any term suggesting the process is independent
quiz.explanation: Section 627.43(2) bans misleading terms about complaint procedures or designated employees, including any term like 'ombudsman' that suggests independence from the bank.

quiz.question: How long must a bank keep its record of a complaint under section 627.44?
options: At least two years
At least seven years
At least five years
Until the complaint is resolved
quiz.explanation: Section 627.44 requires a complaint record retained for at least seven years, accessible to the Commissioner.

quiz.question: A customer's complaint has been open 56 days without a final response from the bank. What can the customer do?
options: Nothing until the bank issues its final response
Ask FCAC to investigate and order compensation
Take the complaint to the external complaints body, OBSI, free of charge
Pay a filing fee to have OBSI review it
quiz.explanation: FCAC's consumer information says a customer may go to OBSI once 56 days have passed or the bank has given its final written response. Section 627.49 requires the body's services to be free for complainants. FCAC does not resolve individual complaints.

quiz.question: Which of these does FCAC's complaint-handling guideline expect a bank's training program to include?
options: Monitoring of employees' training status and tests of whether training works
Training only for designated employees, never for front-line staff who first hear complaints
One induction session with no updates, even when legal requirements later change
An FCAC certificate for each employee before they may handle any customer complaint
quiz.explanation: Both the current and revised guidelines expect initial and ongoing formal training for all employees who deal with complaints, monitoring of training status, measuring and testing effectiveness, and regular updates.

quiz.question: Under FCAC's revised complaint-handling guideline, effective 23 June 2027, what is the expected maximum time to refer a complaint not resolved at first contact to a designated employee?
options: 3 business days from acknowledgement
30 calendar days from the written acknowledgement
56 days, the same as the full complaint period
14 calendar days from when the complaint is first communicated
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 30 of the revised guideline says referral should not exceed 14 calendar days from the date the complaint is first communicated to the bank. This expectation applies from 23 June 2027.

quiz.question: Which of these is wrongdoing under section 979.1 of the Bank Act?
options: A disagreement over the colour of a new branch sign
A breach of the bank's own policy on obtaining customer consent
A colleague's personal opinion about a product's price
A customer's decision to move accounts to another bank
quiz.explanation: Wrongdoing includes contraventions of the Act or regulations, of a voluntary code or public commitment, and of a policy or procedure established by the bank.

quiz.question: A teller reasonably believes a colleague is adding products without consent. To whom may she report under section 979.2?
options: The bank, FCAC, OSFI, another financial regulator or law enforcement
Only to her direct manager, in writing, so that the branch can deal with it first
Only to the bank's external auditor, who must then decide whether to inform FCAC
Only to the media, and only after internal reporting has failed for at least 60 days
quiz.explanation: Section 979.2(1) lists the bank, the Commissioner, the Superintendent, a government body that regulates or supervises financial institutions, and law enforcement.

quiz.question: Two months after an employee reported wrongdoing in good faith, her manager removes her from a promised promotion list 'for being disloyal'. What does the Bank Act say?
options: It is allowed because promotions are at management's discretion under the employment contract
It is allowed if the report later turns out to be unfounded after the bank's investigation
Section 979.4 bans disadvantaging an employee because of such a report
It is a matter only for provincial employment law, since the Bank Act is silent on it
quiz.explanation: Section 979.4(1) prohibits dismissing, suspending, demoting, disciplining, harassing or otherwise disadvantaging an employee, or denying a benefit of employment, because of a report made on reasonable belief.

sessions.title: FCAC enforcement and assessment readiness
sessions.summary: Learn how FCAC supervises and enforces: notices of violation, the penalty criteria and maximums in the FCAC Act, publication, due diligence and compliance agreements. Then assemble the bank's consumer protection training programme, with roles, records and evidence FCAC will expect.
objectives: Describe FCAC's enforcement process from notice of violation to payment, representations or decision
Apply the penalty criteria and maximum penalties in sections 19 and 20 of the FCAC Act
Explain publication, the due diligence defence and compliance agreements
Design a section 627.02 training programme with governance, audience mapping, completion tracking, effectiveness testing and updates
Recall the main regulator expectations tested in the final exam

cards.title: Stage five: the letter from Ottawa
cards.setting: Board room, Aurora Ridge Bank, Toronto. 8:00 am.

lines.text: An FCAC supervisory letter has arrived. FCAC wants evidence of how Aurora Ridge Bank trains staff and third parties on its consumer policies.
This is where our work becomes evidence. FCAC will ask what we teach, to whom, how we know it worked and how we keep it current.
And if they find gaps, what's the worst case?
A notice of violation, a penalty of up to $10 million per violation for a financial institution, and our name published with it.
Then let's walk in with a programme we can defend, not a pile of attendance sheets.

cards.title: How FCAC enforcement works

scenes.heading: Supervision first
scenes.narration: FCAC supervises banks through reporting, reviews and investigations. Banks report complaints and compliance issues, and FCAC uses this information to find problems.

scenes.heading: Notice of violation
scenes.narration: If the Commissioner believes on reasonable grounds that a violation occurred, a notice of violation is served, naming the violation and the proposed penalty.

scenes.heading: Pay or respond
scenes.narration: The bank has 30 days, or a longer period the Commissioner sets, to pay or make representations. Paying means the bank is deemed to have committed the violation.

scenes.heading: Decision
scenes.narration: If the bank makes representations, the Commissioner decides on a balance of probabilities and may impose the proposed penalty, a lesser one or none. Due diligence is a defence.

scenes.heading: Publication
scenes.narration: The Commissioner makes public the nature of the violation, who committed it and the penalty, and may publish the reasons.

cards.title: FCAC penalties against banks, 2023 to 2026
cards.caption: Source: FCAC Decisions and summaries of proceedings. Amounts are penalties, separate from customer refunds.

items.label: TD, card rebates (2024)
items.detail: Summary of proceeding #2: about 255,886 customers affected

items.label: TD, loan payments (2024)
items.detail: Summary #3: amortization extended after payment frequency changes
