cards.question: Under section 20 of the FCAC Act, which of these is a factor in setting a penalty amount?
options: The degree of intention or negligence, the harm done and the duration of the violation
The bank's share price on the day of the notice
Whether the bank's CEO apologised in public
The number of branches the bank has in Quebec
cards.explanation: Section 20 lists intention or negligence, harm, duration, ability to pay, history of violations in the previous five years and any prescribed criteria. Section 20.1 says the purpose is to promote compliance, not to punish.

cards.title: Penalties, purpose and publication
cards.body:
The **Financial Consumer Agency of Canada Act** sets the enforcement tools:

- **Maximum penalty:** **$10 million** per violation for a financial institution and **$1 million** for a natural person (section 19(2)).
- **Criteria** (section 20): intention or negligence, harm, duration, ability to pay, **history** of violations or convictions in the previous **five years**, and prescribed criteria.
- **Purpose** (section 20.1): to **promote compliance**, not to punish.
- **Paying** the proposed penalty means the bank is **deemed to have committed** the violation (section 23).
- **Due diligence** is a defence (section 28), but the bank must show it took **all reasonable steps**. In Decision #139 RBC's training material did not meet that bar.
- **Publication** (section 31): the nature of the violation, the name and the penalty are made public.

In Decision #145 the Commissioner combined a **$1.6 million** penalty on Community Trust Company with a **compliance agreement** to address outstanding issues and remediation.

cards.title: Match the FCAC Act tool to what it does
cards.prompt: Link each provision to its effect.

pairs.right: Caps penalties at $10 million per violation for a financial institution
Lists criteria such as negligence, harm, duration and five-year history
States that penalties aim to promote compliance, not to punish
Paying the proposed penalty means the violation is deemed committed
Makes due diligence a defence to a violation
Requires publication of the violation, the name and the penalty

cards.title: A turn: what counts as evidence?
cards.setting: Nadia's office, the day before the FCAC meeting.

lines.text: We have 97% completion on the consumer protection module. Isn't that enough?
Completion is one line. FCAC's guidelines also expect us to measure whether training works, review it regularly and update it when the law or our procedures change.
And to tailor it: designated complaint employees and whistleblowing report handlers need role-specific training.
Plus third-party sellers. Our card partner's staff and the mortgage brokers have to be on the list too.
Exactly. Let's build the programme map.

cards.title: Layers of Aurora Ridge Bank's consumer protection training
cards.caption: A layered programme meets section 627.02 for everyone and the guidelines' role-specific expectations.

items.label: Board committee and senior management
items.detail: Oversee consumer policies; receive training and complaint metrics

items.label: Designated complaint and whistleblowing roles
items.detail: Role-specific training on investigation, redress, confidentiality

items.label: Sales, lending and product staff
items.detail: Appropriateness, products' features and risks, consent, remuneration rules

items.label: All officers and employees in Canada
items.detail: Core Part XII.2 policies, complaints, whistleblowing, disclosure

items.label: Third parties who offer or sell
items.detail: Same core content, bank's procedures, completion tracked in agreements

cards.title: The FCAC meeting
cards.situation: During the meeting, FCAC staff ask: 'How do you know your section 627.02 training works?' The bank's head of learning starts to answer: 'Everyone clicked through the module, and we have a 97% completion rate.'

choices.text: Step in and present completion data with test results, call and file reviews linked to training topics, complaint trends, and the log of updates made after legal and procedural changes.
choices.outcome: Best choice. FCAC's guidelines expect completion monitoring plus testing of effectiveness and regular review. Linking training to outcomes is the evidence supervisors look for.

choices.text: Offer to send the module's slide deck after the meeting.
choices.outcome: Partly helpful: content matters. But it does not answer the question of effectiveness or show the training is kept current.

choices.text: Point out that the Bank Act does not define 'effective', so completion should be enough.
choices.outcome: Poor. FCAC's guidelines expect measurement and testing of training effectiveness, and a defensive answer weakens any later due diligence defence.

choices.text: Promise that every employee will repeat the module next week.
choices.outcome: Poor. Repeating the same module shows activity, not effectiveness, and does not address gaps.

cards.title: Good evidence or weak evidence?
cards.prompt: Sort what Aurora Ridge Bank could show FCAC about its training.

items.text: Training records for staff and third-party sellers, mapped to roles
Assessment results and follow-up for people who failed
A log showing modules updated after the revised complaint guideline
Call reviews showing staff obtain and confirm express consent
A poster in the staff room saying 'Treat customers fairly'
A slide deck last updated in 2021
An email asking staff to read the Bank Act

cards.question: Aurora Ridge Bank receives a notice of violation and pays the proposed penalty within the time allowed. What follows under the FCAC Act?
options: The bank is deemed to have committed the violation and proceedings in respect of it end
The violation is erased and nothing is published
FCAC must take the bank to court to confirm the violation
The penalty is refunded if the bank fixes the problem
cards.explanation: Section 23(1) says paying the proposed penalty means the person is deemed to have committed the violation and the proceedings end. Section 31 requires publication of the violation, the name and the amount.

cards.title: Readiness checklist: what FCAC expects to see

cards.back: Senior management and the board committee responsible for consumer provisions oversee the policies, as FCAC's guidelines expect.
Every officer and employee in Canada plus third parties who offer or sell, mapped to role-specific content.
The bank's own policies on appropriateness, consent, pressure, disclosure, complaints, whistleblowing and access.
Completion tracked for staff and third parties, with follow-up on gaps.
Testing, quality reviews and complaint data used to judge whether training changes behaviour.
Training refreshed when laws, guidelines or procedures change, such as the June 2027 complaint guideline and, later, section 627.134.

cards.title: Real case: Community Trust and a compliance agreement (2023)
cards.body:
In **Decision #145** (posted November 2023), FCAC staff alleged that **Community Trust Company**, a federally regulated trust company, committed two violations of the Cost of Borrowing (Trust and Loan Companies) Regulations by failing to disclose a fee to discharge a fixed-rate mortgage.

- The Commissioner found both violations occurred and imposed **$1.6 million** for the first and **no penalty** for the second.
- The Commissioner directed FCAC to address outstanding issues, including **more complete remediation**, through a **compliance agreement** with the company.
- The Commissioner considered the penalty, the agreement and the changes already made sufficient to deter and to promote compliance.

**Lesson:** enforcement is not only about fines. FCAC can require structured remediation, and training is often one of the commitments a bank must then deliver and evidence.

cards.title: Final stage take-aways
items: FCAC can issue notices of violation with penalties of up to $10 million per violation for a financial institution and $1 million for an individual.
Penalties weigh negligence, harm, duration, ability to pay and five-year history, and aim to promote compliance, not to punish.
Paying a proposed penalty means the violation is deemed committed; FCAC publishes the violation, the name and the amount.
Due diligence is a defence only if the bank proves it took all reasonable steps, including training that teaches the real requirement.
A defensible programme covers everyone in scope, is role-specific, tracks completion, tests effectiveness and is updated when the law changes.

cards.prompt: If FCAC asked you tomorrow to show how you were trained on the bank's consumer policies, what could you show, and what would you add?

quiz.question: What is the maximum penalty under the FCAC Act for a single violation committed by a financial institution?
options: $10 million
$1 million
$50 million
quiz.explanation: Section 19(2) sets the maximum at $10 million for a violation by a financial institution or payment card network operator and $1 million for a natural person.

quiz.question: After a notice of violation is served, how long does a bank normally have to pay or make representations?
options: 7 days, with no extension
90 days after the next quarterly report
Until FCAC files the matter in Federal Court
30 days after service, or any longer period the Commissioner specifies
quiz.explanation: Under section 22(3) of the FCAC Act, the notice sets out the right to pay or make representations within 30 days after service, or a longer period the Commissioner specifies.

quiz.question: According to section 20.1 of the FCAC Act, what is the purpose of an administrative monetary penalty?
options: To compensate each affected customer directly
To fund FCAC's financial literacy programs
To promote compliance with the consumer provisions, not to punish
To punish senior executives personally
quiz.explanation: Section 20.1 states that the purpose of the penalty is to promote compliance and not to punish. Customer redress is dealt with separately.

quiz.question: In setting a penalty, FCAC considers a bank's history of prior violations within what period before the violation?
options: One year
Five years
Ten years
Since the bank was incorporated
quiz.explanation: Section 20(e) refers to prior violations or convictions under an Act listed in Schedule 1 within the five-year period immediately before the violation.

quiz.question: A bank makes representations after a notice of violation. What can the Commissioner decide?
options: Only whether to double the penalty because the bank chose to contest the notice
Only whether to refer the matter to OSFI for prudential action against the bank
Only to accept the bank's representations as written, without any review of the facts
Decide on a balance of probabilities and impose the penalty, a lesser one or none
quiz.explanation: Section 23(2) requires the Commissioner to decide on a balance of probabilities and allows the proposed penalty, a lesser penalty or no penalty.

quiz.question: What does FCAC make public after a violation is established?
options: The nature of the violation, who committed it and the penalty
Only an anonymous statistic in its annual report to Parliament, with no names
Only the names of the employees involved, not the name of the financial institution
Nothing at all, since FCAC enforcement proceedings are confidential by law
quiz.explanation: Section 31 requires the Commissioner to make public the nature of the violation, the name of the person who committed it and the penalty, and allows publication of reasons.

quiz.question: In Decision #145, what did the Commissioner add to the $1.6 million penalty imposed on Community Trust Company?
options: A ban on the company offering any new mortgages to consumers for five years
A referral to the RCMP so that criminal charges could be laid against its officers
A compliance agreement to address outstanding issues and fuller remediation
An order to close all of its branches and transfer its customers to other lenders
quiz.explanation: The Commissioner directed FCAC to address outstanding issues, including more complete remediation for the second violation, through a compliance agreement.

quiz.question: Mei reports 97% completion of the consumer protection module. What else do FCAC's guidelines expect the bank to be able to show?
options: Nothing more: completion above 90% is the standard FCAC sets in its training guideline
That training effectiveness is tested and the content regularly updated
That each employee signed a statement agreeing with FCAC's interpretation of the law
That the module was reviewed and approved by OSFI before it was launched to staff
quiz.explanation: The appropriateness and complaint-handling guidelines expect monitoring of completion, measuring and testing effectiveness (complaints), and regular review and updates. FCAC sets no completion percentage.

quiz.question: Which group should receive role-specific training under FCAC's complaint-handling and whistleblowing guidelines, beyond the core programme?
options: Only external auditors who review the bank
Designated complaint employees and the employees who deal with reports of wrongdoing
Only customers who have filed more than one complaint
Only the bank's shareholders at the annual meeting
quiz.explanation: The complaint guideline expects training for designated employees to reflect their roles, and the whistleblowing guideline expects specific, tailored training for employees who deal with reports of wrongdoing.

quiz.question: A bank wants to rely on due diligence in an FCAC proceeding over consent failures. What will it most need to show?
options: That it took all reasonable steps, including training that taught the requirement
That the violation affected fewer than 100 customers and caused only a small financial loss
That its staff did not intend to breach the law and acted in good faith at all times
That a competitor had made the same mistake and was not penalised by FCAC for it
quiz.explanation: Section 28 makes due diligence a defence, and FCAC decisions say the bank must provide affirmative proof that it took all reasonable steps. In Decision #139, weak training material and procedures defeated the defence.

regulators: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI), as a whistleblowing channel
Ombudsman for Banking Services and Investments (OBSI), external complaints body

bank.question: Aurora Ridge Bank's internal auditor finds that the training on consumer policies reaches all employees but none of the 300 independent mortgage brokers who sell the bank's mortgages in Canada. What is the most accurate finding?
options: No gap, because section 627.02 only covers the bank's own employees
A gap against section 627.02, which covers any person who offers or sells the bank's products in Canada
No gap, because brokers are supervised only by provincial regulators
A gap only if the brokers earn more than half their income from the bank
bank.explanation: Section 627.02 extends the training duty to any person who offers or sells the institution's products or services in Canada. Provincial licensing of brokers does not remove the bank's own duty.

bank.question: Which statement best describes how FCAC guidelines relate to the Bank Act consumer provisions?
options: They replace the Bank Act wherever the two differ, because guidelines are more recent and detailed
They are optional suggestions with no supervisory weight, which banks may ignore without consequence
They state FCAC's expectations; if an older one conflicts with the framework, the framework prevails
They apply only to provincially regulated credit unions and not to federally regulated banks
bank.explanation: FCAC describes guidelines as its expectations for meeting market conduct obligations, and states that after 30 June 2022 the Framework Requirements prevail over any inconsistent guideline.

bank.question: A product manager in Toronto changes the fee rules for a chequing account but never attends any consumer protection training because she 'never talks to customers'. Which response is most accurate?
options: As an employee in Canada, section 627.02 requires her to be trained on consumer policies
She is exempt because section 627.02 names only staff who deal with customers in branches
She needs training only if FCAC names her personally in a notice of violation against the bank
She is exempt as long as her manager has been trained and approves every fee change she makes
bank.explanation: Section 627.02 covers officers and employees in Canada without limiting the duty to customer-facing roles. Staff who design fees and disclosures directly shape compliance.

bank.question: Which pair of agencies supervises a Canadian federally regulated bank for consumer conduct and for prudential soundness respectively?
options: OSFI for consumer conduct and FCAC for prudential soundness
FINTRAC for consumer conduct and OSFI for prudential soundness
OBSI for consumer conduct and FCAC for prudential soundness
FCAC for consumer conduct and OSFI for prudential soundness
bank.explanation: FCAC supervises compliance with the consumer provisions; OSFI is the prudential supervisor. FINTRAC handles AML/ATF and OBSI is the external complaints body, not a supervisor.

bank.question: Aurora Ridge Bank uses an affiliate that is a finance entity to sell its credit cards. Under section 627.15, which arrangement must be in place?
options: Affiliate staff must report wrongdoing only to the affiliate's own auditors, never to the bank or FCAC
The affiliate must register separately with FCAC as a bank before it may sell any credit cards
The affiliate's customers must complain only to the affiliate, and may never use the bank's process
Affiliate staff can use the bank's whistleblowing procedures and are protected from retaliation
bank.explanation: Section 627.15 requires, among other things, that the affiliate's employees can report under section 979.2 and access the procedures under section 979.3, and that the affiliate complies with section 979.4. Customers must also have access to the bank's complaint procedures.

bank.question: In the TD card rebate case (FCAC summary of proceeding #2, 2024), which regulations had TD breached for the period after 30 June 2022?
options: The Negative Option Billing Regulations
The Cost of Borrowing (Trust and Loan Companies) Regulations
The Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations
The Access to Basic Banking Services Regulations
bank.explanation: FCAC said TD violated the Cost of Borrowing (Banks) Regulations up to 29 June 2022 and the Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations from 30 June 2022 to 5 October 2023, showing the framework replaced the older regulations.

bank.question: A compliance lead argues: 'If a procedure is written down, we have met our obligations, even if staff don't follow it.' Which FCAC case most directly contradicts this view?
options: BMO (2025), where FCAC cited inconsistent employee adherence to procedures and controls that failed to detect it
Scotiabank (2021), where no penalty was imposed for a short violation
Community Trust (2023), where FCAC required a compliance agreement
National Bank (2023), where systems failed to process interest on non-business days
bank.explanation: In summary of proceeding #4, FCAC identified inconsistent employee adherence with procedures, and monitoring that failed to detect it, as root causes of BMO's violations.

bank.question: Which description of section 627.02 of the Bank Act is most accurate?
options: It sets a mandatory eight-hour annual course whose content FCAC approves before it is delivered
It requires training on the bank's own consumer policies but sets no course length or cycle
It requires a provincial licence for every bank employee who discusses products with customers
It requires training only when FCAC asks for it in writing after finding a compliance problem
bank.explanation: Section 627.02 requires training on the policies and procedures the institution has established for complying with the consumer provisions. It does not prescribe hours, frequency or FCAC approval; FCAC guidelines add expectations of initial and ongoing training.

bank.question: A contact centre agent calls the same customer five times in a week about a credit card offer after she has said no twice. Which Bank Act concept is most clearly engaged?
options: Undue pressure, meaning pressure that is reasonably considered excessive or persistent in the circumstances
Preferential pricing, which section 627.05 expressly allows
The information box, which section 627.57 requires
The renewal notice, which section 627.6 requires
bank.explanation: Persistent contact after a clear refusal fits the definition of undue pressure in section 627.01, which section 627.04 prohibits.

bank.question: A borrower must provide home insurance as security for a mortgage. The bank says it must approve the insurer. When is that lawful?
options: Never: any requirement about the security for a loan is coercive tied selling under section 627.04
Only if the borrower buys the insurance from the bank's own affiliate at the bank's posted price
Only if FCAC approves each insurer in advance and publishes the list on its website
When the bank's approval of the product is not unreasonably withheld, as section 627.05(3) allows
bank.explanation: Section 627.05(3) lets the bank require that a product obtained as security for a loan meet its approval, provided approval is not unreasonably withheld. Requiring the affiliate's product would risk coercive tied selling.

bank.question: A customer asks for a specific high-fee premium credit card. Under FCAC's appropriateness guideline, what should the adviser do?
options: Sell it without any assessment, because the customer asked for it and has the final say
Refuse it outright, because premium cards are never appropriate for individual customers
Still assess appropriateness and tell the customer clearly if it is not appropriate
Ask FCAC to approve the sale before proceeding, since the card carries a high annual fee
bank.explanation: Paragraph 19 expects an assessment even when consumers request the product, and paragraph 22 expects the bank to inform them when a product is assessed as not appropriate.

bank.question: Mei redesigns the sales scorecard. Which design best fits section 627.07 and paragraphs 23-24 of FCAC's appropriateness guideline?
options: Bonuses based only on the number of products sold per customer, paid monthly to each adviser
Bonuses doubled for products with the highest fees, to reward advisers who grow revenue fastest
Bonuses that mix sales with quality measures such as appropriateness reviews
No review of incentives once sales leaders approve them, to keep the scheme stable for staff
bank.explanation: Section 627.07 requires remuneration that does not interfere with appropriateness policies, and FCAC expects remuneration metrics to align with appropriateness and to be reviewed regularly.

bank.question: Under FCAC's appropriateness guideline, which of the following should be covered when a bank trains people who offer or sell its products?
options: The features, charges, risks and benefits of the products and how to explain them to consumers
The bank's share price history and dividend policy
Techniques for closing sales before the customer reads the agreement
Only the bank's internal IT systems, without product content
bank.explanation: Paragraph 17 expects training on the bank's appropriateness obligations and on the products sold, including their features, charges, risks and benefits and how to explain them.

bank.question: Rogers Bank (Decision #140, 2021) was penalised for credit card sales. What did the regulations then in force require that Rogers Bank failed to do?
options: Publish its complaint statistics within 135 days
Obtain express consent before providing cards and confirm oral consent in writing
Give six months' notice before closing a rural branch
Open accounts without a minimum deposit
bank.explanation: The Commissioner found two violations of the Negative Option Billing Regulations: providing credit cards without express consent and failing to confirm oral consent in writing. The penalties totalled $250,000.

bank.question: Which statement about consent under sections 627.08 and 627.09 is correct?
options: Consent may be inferred if the customer does not object within 30 days of receiving the product
Consent requests must be clear and not misleading, and the agreement comes first
Consent requests may use any wording the bank chooses, as long as they are sent in writing
A product may be provided first and the agreement signed later, once the customer has used it
bank.explanation: Section 627.08 requires express consent and an agreement before providing a product, and section 627.09 requires consent requests to be clear, simple and not misleading. Silence or use is not consent.

bank.question: A bank charges a customer an annual fee that her agreement does not provide for. Once this is discovered, what does Division 4 of Part XII.2 require?
options: The bank may keep the fee if it was disclosed on a website
The customer must take the matter to court to recover it
The bank need only apologise if the fee was small
The bank must credit or refund the charge
bank.explanation: Section 627.997 requires the bank to credit or refund a charge or penalty that was not provided for in an agreement, or the excess where it was greater than agreed.

bank.question: Under section 627.06, which customers and products does the appropriateness duty cover?
options: Only products sold to corporations with more than 500 employees and large credit facilities
Only investment products sold outside Canada to customers who are not Canadian residents
Products offered or sold in Canada to individuals for non-business purposes
Every product the bank sells, including loans and accounts provided to large businesses
bank.explanation: Section 627.06 applies to products or services in Canada that the bank offers or sells to a natural person other than for business purposes.

bank.question: A teller refuses a retail deposit account to a newcomer to Canada who presents a foreign passport and a recent Canadian utility bill showing name and address. What is the best assessment?
options: The refusal is correct, because a foreign passport is never acceptable identification for an account
The refusal is correct, because newcomers must live in Canada for six months before opening one
The refusal is correct, because the person has no Canadian credit history the bank can review
Likely wrong: these can be two reliable documents and no refusal ground is evident
bank.explanation: Section 627.17(1)(a)(i) lists foreign passports and recent Canadian utility bills among documents from a reliable source. Credit history and recent arrival are not refusal grounds under section 627.18.

bank.question: Which document must a member bank give a person whose request for a retail deposit account it refuses?
options: A copy of the person's credit report and the score the bank used to make its decision
A copy of the suspicious transaction report the bank must file with FINTRAC for each refusal
A written refusal with its complaint procedures and contact details for OBSI and FCAC
A referral letter to a provincial credit union that must then open an account for the person
bank.explanation: Section 627.19 requires a written statement that the account will not be opened and the information in section 627.65(a) to (c): complaint procedures, the external complaints body's name and contact, and FCAC's contact details.

bank.question: A rural branch has another retail deposit-taking branch 6 km away by road. How much notice must the bank give customers and the public before closing it?
options: At least six months' written notice plus a newspaper notice
At least four months' written notice
At least 30 days' notice on the bank's website
No notice, because another branch is nearby
bank.explanation: Section 627.993(1)(b) requires four months' notice for urban branches or rural branches with another branch within 10 km travelling distance. Six months applies only when no such branch exists.

bank.question: A savings advertisement shows '5% interest' in large type; small print says the rate applies for 30 days only on new deposits over $250,000. Which provision is most at risk?
options: Section 627.17, which requires basic accounts to be opened
Section 627.14, which requires advertisements to be accurate, clear and not misleading
Section 979.4, which prohibits retaliation
Section 627.46, which requires quarterly complaint reports
bank.explanation: Section 627.14 requires any advertisement in Canada by the bank to be accurate, clear and not misleading. A headline rate that most savers cannot get is a classic misleading-advertising risk.

bank.question: Once section 627.134 is in force, which of the following must a bank's consumer-targeted fraud policies set out?
options: A fixed reimbursement percentage, set by FCAC, that applies to every fraud loss in the same way
A promise never to suspend or delay any customer transaction, even one that looks suspicious
A list of the names of all fraud victims, published on the bank's website once a year
Criteria for deciding when a transaction is suspicious and when a victim has a remedy
bank.explanation: Section 627.134(2) will require criteria for suspicious transactions, for suspending or cancelling them, for deciding whether a person is a victim and what remedies are available, and how decisions are communicated. Victim identities in reports are confidential.

bank.question: A customer is tricked by a scammer posing as police into authorising a transfer from his account. Under the amended Bank Act definition (not yet in force), is this consumer-targeted fraud?
options: Yes, because the definition includes transactions authorized as a result of coercion or deception
No, because the customer authorised the transfer himself
No, because only card transactions are covered
Yes, but only if the amount exceeds $10,000
bank.explanation: The definition added to section 627.01(1) covers transactions that are unauthorized or authorized as a result of coercion or deception, which captures this kind of impersonation scam.

bank.question: What is the legal status of the Bank Act's consumer-targeted fraud training duty in November 2026?
options: Enacted in 2026 but not yet in force, pending a coming-into-force date
In force since the framework began on 30 June 2022
In force since FCAC's revised complaint guideline was published
Withdrawn before Royal Assent and never enacted
bank.explanation: Section 627.134 was added by S.C. 2026, c. 3 (assented 26 March 2026) and appears among the amendments not in force in the official consolidation.

bank.question: In which situation does section 627.57 require staff to draw attention orally to the information box?
options: When a customer visits a branch to ask for branch hours
When the bank sends a monthly statement by mail
When the bank solicits an application for the product by telephone or the customer phones to apply
Whenever the customer opens the bank's mobile app
bank.explanation: Section 627.57(2) requires the bank to orally draw attention to the information box when it solicits applications by telephone or a person phones to apply.

bank.question: In TD's 2024 loan payment case (FCAC summary of proceeding #3), what was the disclosure problem?
options: TD advertised mortgage rates that were never actually available to most of its customers
TD refused to open deposit accounts for people who had been bankrupt in the past seven years
TD failed to report its complaint records to FCAC within 60 days after each quarter
A payment frequency change extended amortization without clear disclosure
bank.explanation: FCAC found that a calculation error after payment frequency changes extended amortization, with financial implications not disclosed. TD paid a $5.5 million penalty.

bank.question: A customer posts on the bank's social media page, under a nickname, that a branch charged him a fee he never agreed to. Under FCAC's complaint-handling guideline, what should the bank do?
options: Ignore it, because only signed letters count as complaints
Respond and offer access to its complaint process; if he stays unnamed, still record the complaint
Delete the post and report the account to FCAC
Ask OBSI to deal with it directly
bank.explanation: FCAC's guideline expects banks to respond to complainants who have not given their name, offer access to the process and, if they remain unidentified, create a record with the information available.

bank.question: Within what time after the end of each quarter must a bank report to FCAC on complaints dealt with by its designated employees?
options: 60 days
10 days
30 days
135 days
bank.explanation: Section 627.46 requires the quarterly submission within 60 days after the end of each quarter. 135 days is the deadline for annual public complaint information under section 627.47.

bank.question: OBSI decides that part of a complaint falls outside its terms of reference. What must it do under section 627.49?
options: Return the complaint to the bank without telling the customer why it was not accepted
Refer the complaint to the Federal Court within 90 days for a decision on its merits
Charge the customer a fee to review the out-of-scope part anyway, at the customer's choice
Give written reasons and name any other body to approach, within 30 days
bank.explanation: Section 627.49(e) requires written reasons and the name of any other entity to approach within 30 days after the external complaints body receives the complaint.

bank.question: A front-line employee who cannot settle a complaint asks a designated employee for help. Under FCAC's revised complaint-handling guideline, what is the consequence?
options: Nothing changes until the customer writes to the bank
The 56-day period stops while the designated employee reviews it
The complaint is treated as referred to a designated employee and must be reported to FCAC
The complaint must go straight to OBSI
bank.explanation: Paragraph 34 of the revised guideline says input or assistance from a designated employee means the complaint is considered referred, so the bank must report it. The 56-day period is not paused.

bank.question: Under FCAC's revised complaint-handling guideline (effective 23 June 2027), what must a Notice of Final Decision include?
options: The final decision, its reasons and the customer's right to go to OBSI
A waiver of the customer's right to go to OBSI, signed by the customer to close the file
A copy of the bank's annual report and its public accountability statement for the year
An FCAC approval stamp confirming that the regulator agrees with the bank's decision
bank.explanation: Paragraph 52 expects the notice to include the facts, the timeframe, the final decision and how it was reached, the redress method if any, and information on the customer's right to go to the external complaints body.

bank.question: Priya discovers that 40 complaints in a month concern the same incorrect overdraft fee. What do FCAC's complaint-handling expectations call for beyond fixing each complaint?
options: Close each complaint quickly so the quarterly numbers look better
Analyse the root cause, check whether other customers were harmed and provide redress to all affected
Wait until OBSI identifies a systemic issue
Refund only those customers who complained
bank.explanation: FCAC expects complaint data to be analysed for recurring and systemic issues; the revised guideline expects root cause analysis and redress or remediation for all affected consumers.

bank.question: Under section 979.2, when may the bank disclose a whistleblower's identity to FCAC, OSFI, another regulator or law enforcement?
options: When that body deems it needed for an investigation; the bank must try to tell the employee
Whenever the employee's manager requests it in order to deal with the matter at branch level
Only after the employee has left the bank and signed a release allowing the disclosure
Never, under any circumstances, even when an investigation by law enforcement requires it
bank.explanation: Section 979.2(3) allows disclosure when the receiving authority considers it necessary for an investigation, and section 979.2(5) requires every reasonable effort to inform the employee.

bank.question: FCAC's whistleblowing guideline expects training to be focused in particular on which employees?
options: Only employees who have already filed a report of wrongdoing at some point in the past
Those whose roles give them more chance to witness or contribute to wrongdoing
Only new hires during their first week, since longer-serving staff already know the process
Only staff based outside Canada, who are not otherwise covered by the Bank Act
bank.explanation: Paragraph 12 of the guideline expects regular and ongoing training for all employees, tailored training for those who handle reports, and a focus on employees whose roles give greater opportunity to witness, detect or contribute to wrongdoing.

bank.question: An investigation of a whistleblowing report reveals a breach of a consumer provision. What does FCAC's whistleblowing guideline expect?
options: The bank keeps the breach internal to protect the whistleblower
The bank waits for a customer complaint before acting
The bank assesses whether to report the breach to FCAC and, if it reports, says it learned of it through whistleblowing
The bank reports the employee's name to FCAC in every case
bank.explanation: Paragraph 32 expects the bank to assess reporting the breach under FCAC's regulatory reporting guide and, when reporting, to identify that it became aware of it through a whistleblowing report.

bank.question: A bank neither pays the proposed penalty nor makes representations within the time in a notice of violation. What follows under the FCAC Act?
options: It is deemed to have committed it; the Commissioner sets the penalty, up to that proposed
The notice lapses after the deadline and the matter is closed without any finding
FCAC must start criminal proceedings instead, because the administrative route has ended
The penalty is automatically doubled and collected through the Federal Court of Canada
bank.explanation: Section 23(3) says a person who neither pays nor makes representations is deemed to have committed the violation, and the Commissioner may impose the proposed penalty, a lesser one or none.

bank.question: An individual employee, not the bank, commits a violation of a consumer provision designated under the FCAC Act. What is the maximum penalty?
options: $1 million
$10 million
bank.explanation: Section 19(2) sets a maximum of $1 million for a violation by a natural person and $10 million for a financial institution.

bank.question: FCAC is setting a penalty for a bank whose card statements were wrong for two decades and affected many customers, with an earlier violation three years before. Which factors under section 20 weigh most heavily?
options: Only the bank's ability to pay, since the purpose is to punish
Only whether the bank's staff intended the error
Negligence, the harm done, the long duration and the history of prior violations within five years
Only the number of customers who complained to OBSI
bank.explanation: Section 20 lists negligence or intention, harm, duration, ability to pay and five-year history. FCAC's summaries for TD and RBC cited long duration, harm and history. Section 20.1 says the purpose is not to punish.

bank.question: Which record would best support a bank's due diligence defence in a consent-related FCAC proceeding?
options: A board resolution stating that the bank values its customers and expects staff to act fairly
Evidence that the bank's competitors had similar consent problems during the same period
A statement from the legal department that no customer has ever sued the bank over consent
Training and scripts teaching consent in every channel, with monitoring results
bank.explanation: Due diligence requires proof that the bank took all reasonable steps. Decision #139 shows that FCAC reviews training material, scripts and call recordings to see whether consent requirements were clearly taught and followed.

bank.question: Which of the following is the best summary of how FCAC expects banks to manage consumer protection training across its guidelines?
options: One mandatory module at hiring, with no further obligations once staff have passed it
Training only after FCAC issues a notice of violation that identifies a gap in knowledge
Training only for staff who sell credit products, since deposits carry little consumer risk
Initial and ongoing training, completion tracking, testing, updates and role content
bank.explanation: The appropriateness, complaint-handling and whistleblowing guidelines all expect initial and ongoing or regular training, with completion monitoring, review and updating. The complaint guideline adds effectiveness testing, and the complaint and whistleblowing guidelines add role-specific training.

bank.question: Under the FCAC guidelines on appropriate products, complaint handling and whistleblowing, which body is expected to oversee the bank's policies and procedures?
options: The external complaints body, OBSI, which reviews each bank's policies once a year
The bank's largest shareholders, voting on the policies at the annual general meeting
Senior management and the board committee responsible for consumer compliance
FCAC's Consumer Information Centre, which approves policies before they take effect
bank.explanation: Each guideline says the bank's senior management and the board committee responsible for consumer provision compliance (or senior management of an authorized foreign bank) should oversee the policies and procedures.

bank.question: Aurora Ridge Bank must update its training plan for 2027. Which change is required to keep content accurate?
options: Update complaint training for the revised FCAC guideline effective 23 June 2027 and track the status of section 627.134
Remove all whistleblowing content because the rules were repealed in 2026
Replace the 56-day complaint period with 90 days
Stop training third-party sellers, who were removed from section 627.02
bank.explanation: FCAC's revised complaint-handling guideline takes effect on 23 June 2027 and both versions expect training to be updated when requirements change. Section 627.134 is enacted but not yet in force. The other changes are not in the law.
